newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Cohen urges Bulgaria to speed military reforms.
newsitem.headline: Cohen urges Bulgaria to speed military reforms.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen held talks with Bulgarian leaders on Sunday and urged the former hardline Soviet ally to speed up military reform in its quest to join NATO.

Cohen had lunch with President Petar Stoyanov and said after a meeting with Defence Minister Georgi Ananiev that Washington was impressed with recent reforms by democratic Bulgaria, including a free-market economy and respect for human rights.

"The military is currently going to go through some downsizing," he told reporters. "It will be important as that downsizing takes place that it be reformed in a way that would still maintain an effective capability...to defend Bulgaria, but also to provide assistance to other NATO countries consistent with Article 5 of the NATO charter."

Bulgaria is anxious to join NATO, but needs to cut its Soviet-model military and assure continued civilian control over the armed forces, according to U.S. officials who travelled with Cohen to Sofia at the end of a trip to promote military reform in Eastern Europe.
"We believe that Bulgaria plays a key role in helping to stabilise the (Balkans) region," Cohen said.
"Your visit here is a real support for the new political majority which has to overcome serious difficulties that come from seven years of political and economic stagnation," Ananiev told Cohen.
Ananiev called the visit "a guarantee for the irreversibility of the process of NATO enlargement."
NATO last week invited Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join, and suggested that Slovenia and Bulgaria's neighbour Romania might be front-runners for for membership in the future.

The U.S. officials, who asked not to be identified, said they were watching closely to see how Bulgaria's plan to cut its military force from 96.000 troops to about 65,000 within a year will be handled.

Cohen said the United States was anxious to help but no concrete figures were mentioned in discussions about possible additional military aid to the approximately $6 million which Sofia now gets from Washington.
Bulgaria also receives about $35 million annually in U.S. Agency for International Development (AID) help for medical and other civilian projects.

Bulgaria's economic reforms this year have dramatically slashed inflation from nearly 500 per cent to less than 15 percent. The country, which was one of Moscow's closest allies during the Cold War, is an active member of NATO's "Partnership for Peace" military cooperation programme.
Bulgaria is considered a key state in the Balkan region because of its central position, sharing common borders with Greece, Turkey, Macedonia, Romania and Serbia.

"You have to pay attention to the little guys (like Bulgaria) because they can create a lot of problems" if they are not stable cconomically and militarily, one U.S. official told reporters travelling with Cohen.
